title: Daily Temperatures
statement:
`temperatures[i]` is the temperature recorded on day `i`.

Return an array `answer` of the same length where `answer[i]` is the number of days you must wait after day `i` until a **strictly warmer** day. If no later day is warmer, `answer[i]` is `0`.
hints: The brute force scans forward from every day. When a warm day arrives, which earlier days does it answer all at once?

A new temperature resolves every still-waiting earlier day that is colder than it — and those are always the most recent waiting days. Keep the waiting days' indices on a stack; their temperatures never increase toward the top (a monotonic stack).
For each day i: while the stack is non-empty and the day on top is colder than today, pop it as j and set answer[j] = i - j. Then push i. Days left on the stack at the end keep answer 0.
followups: Can you do it scanning right to left, using answers you've already computed to jump ahead?
How does the same idea give the next greater element in a circular array?
If temperatures were limited to 30..100, what other O(n · range) approach becomes possible?
explain: Keep a stack of indices of days that haven't yet seen a warmer day. Their temperatures are non-increasing from bottom to top, because any warmer day would already have popped the colder ones beneath it. For each new day i, pop every index j whose temperature is strictly lower and record answer[j] = i - j, then push i. Every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n) even though there's a nested while loop; space is O(n) for the stack. Use strict < when popping, so equal temperatures keep waiting. In Java an int[] used as a stack (or ArrayDeque<Integer>) beats the legacy Stack class. Scanning forward from every day is O(n^2) on a falling sequence that only warms up at the very end.
